articles.title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Early testers are raving about what Instinct can do, but some say the AI assistant’s sweeping access, broad terms and ability to act on users’ behalf come with uncomfortable trade-offs.
articles.body:
Everyone is buzzing about Instinct , an AI personal assistant still in private access, not only for its incredible capabilities, but also for its potential privacy concerns. The agent, a veritable taskmaster, has been praised as feeling “like magic” and being one of the “most exciting launches” since OpenClaw. However, some testers have also raised concerns about the AI agent’s security model and its worrisome terms of service .

To be fair, Instinct is still in private testing for now, so these concerns haven’t yet scaled to the wider public at this time.

Created by a small team led by former Sierra research scientist Noah Shinn , San Francisco-based Instinct is operated by Spear Street Technology, per its terms and California business filings . It’s currently operating in stealth, per PitchBook .

The AI agent itself works by connecting to your applications and devices, including your email, messaging apps, calendar, and your device’s audio, location, screen, and more. You can text the agent or call it via text message or WhatsApp, asking it to perform various tasks for you, like booking your appointments and reservations, scheduling a ride to the airport, cleaning up your inbox, organizing important information, handling your shopping, finding you cheap flights, and much more.

Though Instinct is described by testers as outperforming their expectations, some have also raised concerns about the company’s approach to customer privacy and security. This raises a timely question: Are the trade-offs of giving AI this level of access and autonomy actually worth it?

For instance, several people are circulating screenshots from the company’s Terms of Service , which grant Instinct a broad “perpetual and irrevocable” license to “access, use, host, cache, store, reproduce, transmit, display, publish, distribute, and modify” any of the user’s materials, including for training its AI models. The terms also detail how Instinct can receive information from users’ devices, including screen captures, cursor movements, and keyboard inputs.

The terms also allow Instinct to enter into “agreements, commitments, or transactions” on users’ behalf, which would be binding.

One early adopter, Peter Yang, pointed out that Instinct would not delete his Gmail records when asked. (The team later fixed the problem by adding a tool for deleting external data in its settings, he said.)

Another person, Claire Vo, found that Instinct was still summarizing their inbox after disconnecting its access . When she asked Instinct what happened, the bot confirmed that the emails were stored in plain text for later searches.

Many others questioned the security model, too. One tester was a bit worried when they found that Instinct was able to pull a sign-up code from their email inbox to complete a particular task — in their case, booking a table at a restaurant via Resy. And Hello Patient co-founder Alex Cohen wrote that once he found out how easily Instinct could be phished , he deleted his account:

In addition, Moxxie Ventures founder Katie Jacobs Stanton shared that Instinct broke her trust when it sent an email on her behalf without first checking with her.

“We’re trading privacy and control for hyper-personalized AI tools (AI notetakers, personalized AI agents, etc), often without fully understanding the trade,” she remarked on X, summarizing the dilemma posed personal AI agents. “The more powerful these agents become, the more trust matters. Every successful action earns a little more trust. One unauthorized action can reset that trust to zero,” she said.

Michael Mignano, the founder of Anchor, which was acquired by Spotify, and now a GP at Union Square Ventures, noted that products like Instinct are going to “change modern security norms for consumers,” adding that “people will increasingly hand over passwords to 3p [third-party] apps, unaware of how or what they are storing for them.”

Interest in Instinct and personal AI has been growing since the arrival of OpenClaw, a personal AI assistant that became popular for its powerful capabilities, leading its founder to join OpenAI to help work on the next generation of personal agents. Another messaging-based assistant, Poke, also just exited to Cognition .

Amid the criticism, Instinct’s team hasn’t yet responded to anyone’s concerns or complaints on X, preferring to keep a low profile . (The bot itself identifies Luca Borletti, also formerly of Sierra, as being involved with the company, but that has not been confirmed.) TechCrunch has heard from multiple investors that Kleiner Perkins and Conviction have invested in the startup and those rounds have now closed.

Requests for comment sent to both the startup’s main email address and Shinn directly have not yet been returned.

articles.title: Card skimming scam is stealing food benefits nationwide
articles.summary: A single card skimmer can generate $1 million in stolen funds, and Secret Service video shows criminals installing them in under two seconds.
articles.body: You swipe your card at the checkout, grab your receipt and walk away. Nothing looks unusual. However, a device sitting right on top of that payment terminal may have copied your card information and PIN. U.S. Secret Service agents recently swept hundreds of retailers across Los Angeles looking for skimmers. What they found shows how sophisticated these devices have become and how difficult they can be to spot. This card skimming scam is especially serious for people who rely on Electronic Benefit Transfer, or EBT, cards. Many of those cards still depend on magnetic-stripe technology that criminals know how to exploit. INSIDE NYC'S 'PERFECT SCAM': LUXURY CARS, DUSTY SHELVES AND THE EBT SECRET BEHIND THE COUNTER New! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward. Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com. Secret Service finds skimmers hiding in plain sight One of the most unsettling parts of the investigation is how quickly criminals can install a skimmer. Surveillance video from the investigation captured a suspect placing one over a payment terminal in less than two seconds. From there, the fake reader sits directly over the real terminal. When someone swipes a card, the device can capture account information and the PIN used during the transaction. We have previously shown you how skimmers and shimmers can steal your payment information. What stands out now is how convincing these newer devices can look. During the Secret Service sweep, agents found a skimmer that blended closely into the legitimate payment terminal. It even had what appeared to be a security hologram. Agents had to pry the device off. Inside, they found miniature electronics and a wireless transmitter. That transmitter can send stolen information to a criminal nearby. The person who installed the skimmer may not have to return and remove it to collect the data. A single skimmer could lead to huge losses The numbers behind this crime are staggering. The Secret Service says a single skimmer can generate as much as $1 million in stolen funds. Across the country, 32 active federal investigations span 15 states. Meanwhile, the Secret Service estimates that skimming costs consumers and financial institutions more than $1 billion each year. The agency has also stepped up its nationwide enforcement efforts. During 2025 operations, law enforcement removed more than 400 illegal skimming devices. The Secret Service says skimming activity has increasingly targeted EBT cards. A recent Los Angeles sweep shows how widespread the problem has become. Law enforcement visited 328 businesses and inspected 1,749 payment devices. Agents seized 16 skimmers. The Secret Service estimated those removals prevented about $16.6 million in potential fraud losses. Why criminals are targeting EBT cards This is where things take a troubling turn. The Secret Service says criminals intentionally target locations with heavy EBT use. That includes stores where people use government benefits to buy groceries. Many credit and debit cards now offer chips or contactless payment. However, many EBT transactions still require a magnetic-stripe swipe. That gives criminals an opening. A skimmer can capture the information stored on the magnetic stripe. Criminals can then copy that information onto another magnetic-stripe card. If they also capture the victim's PIN, they can use the cloned card to steal benefits. For people who rely on those benefits, the impact can be immediate. Victims may discover their accounts have been drained when they try to buy groceries or pay for everyday necessities. Recovering stolen benefits can also take time, leaving families without money they were counting on. VENEZUELAN NATIONALS CHARGED IN $529K ATM JACKPOTTING SCHEME AT I-95 REST STOPS, FEDS SAY Why EBT card security is changing Federal officials know the magnetic stripe is a weak point. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food and Nutrition Service says EBT fraud involving skimming is rising. The agency is working with states on modernizing SNAP EBT systems, including introducing chip cards. Chip technology makes card information harder to copy than data stored on a magnetic stripe. Still, that transition takes time. Until more EBT systems support newer payment technology, millions of people may continue using cards that require a swipe. That leaves benefit recipients with fewer ways to avoid the very payment method criminals are targeting. Organized crime groups are behind some skimming operations The Secret Service says organized criminal groups are involved in some of these skimming schemes. Investigators have linked some operations to groups that travel into the United States and move between locations installing devices. The agency has been conducting skimming operations across the country throughout 2026. Recent sweeps have focused on payment terminals at stores and ATMs where skimming activity is suspected. That kind of coordinated activity can make the devices harder to track and allow criminals to target multiple locations in a short period of time. How to protect yourself from card skimmers You may never spot a well-made skimmer by sight alone. Still, you can lower your risk and catch suspicious activity faster. 1) Tap instead of swiping when you can If a payment terminal supports contactless payments, use them. The Secret Service recommends tap-to-pay when possible. You can also use a digital wallet on your phone if the retailer supports it. For more ways to protect your cards in stores and online, see our guide on how to protect your credit and bank cards from getting hacked. 2) Inspect the payment terminal first Take a few seconds before inserting or swiping your card. Look for a reader that appears loose or crooked. Also watch for damage, unusual gaps or parts that do not seem to line up correctly. The Secret Service recommends avoiding a reader if something looks altered or damaged. IDENTITY THEFT RARELY ANNOUNCES ITSELF: 6 SIGNS YOU MISSED 3) Give the reader a gentle pull Some overlay skimmers sit directly on top of the legitimate card reader. Before swiping, gently check whether anything feels loose or moves unexpectedly. Do not try to rip apart a terminal. If something seems suspicious, stop using it and notify the store. 4) Cover the keypad when entering your PIN A skimmer may capture card information while another device records your PIN. Use your hand to shield the keypad whenever you enter a PIN. That simple habit can make captured card information less useful to a criminal. 5) Turn on transaction alerts Enable alerts through your bank or card issuer so you know when your card gets used. Pay attention to small charges too. If you see something you do not recognize, contact your financial institution using the number on your card or its official app. If money has already disappeared from an account, follow our steps on what to do if your bank account is hacked. 6) Check your EBT balance regularly EBT users should review their account history for transactions they do not recognize. The Food and Nutrition Service recommends checking EBT accounts regularly. It also advises changing your PIN at least once a month, particularly before your benefits are issued. If you spot an unauthorized transaction, change your PIN immediately and contact your state EBT agency. 7) Never share your EBT PIN Government agencies should not need your PIN to verify your eligibility. Do not provide your EBT card number or PIN in response to an unexpected text, phone call or email. Federal officials warn that criminals use several methods to steal benefit information, so protecting the PIN remains important even when no physical skimmer is involved. What to do if you think a skimmer stole your card information Act quickly once you notice suspicious transactions. Kurt's key takeaways What bothers me most about this scam is that criminals are going after people who may have the fewest options to protect themselves. If I can tap my credit card or pay with my phone, I can avoid swiping altogether. Many EBT users cannot make that same choice because their cards still rely on older magnetic-stripe technology. That needs to change. These skimmers have become convincing enough to fool almost anyone, and some can transmit stolen information without the criminal ever coming back for the device. You can check the reader and keep an eye on your account, but there is only so much you can do when the payment system itself leaves you exposed. Moving benefit cards to more secure technology should be a priority, especially when families are depending on that money for food. Have you ever found a suspicious card reader or discovered money missing after using your card, and do you think stores should be required to inspect their payment terminals every day? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com Sign up for my FREE CyberGuy Report CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Copyright 2026 CyberGuy.com. All rights reserved.

Many of those cards still depend on magnetic-stripe technology that criminals know how to exploit. INSIDE NYC'S 'PERFECT SCAM': LUXURY CARS, DUSTY SHELVES AND THE EBT SECRET BEHIND THE COUNTER New! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward. Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com. Secret Service finds skimmers hiding in plain sight One of the most unsettling parts of the investigation is how quickly criminals can install a skimmer. Surveillance video from the investigation captured a suspect placing one over a payment terminal in less than two seconds. From there, the fake reader sits directly over the real terminal. When someone swipes a card, the device can capture account information and the PIN used during the transaction. We have previously shown you how skimmers and shimmers can steal your payment information. What stands out now is how convincing these newer devices can look. During the Secret Service sweep, agents found a skimmer that blended closely into the legitimate payment terminal. It even had what appeared to be a security hologram. Agents had to pry the device off. Inside, they found miniature electronics and a wireless transmitter. That transmitter can send stolen information to a criminal nearby. The person who installed the skimmer may not have to return and remove it to collect the data. A single skimmer could lead to huge losses The numbers behind this crime are staggering. The Secret Service says a single skimmer can generate as much as $1 million in stolen funds. Across the country, 32 active federal investigations span 15 states. Meanwhile, the Secret Service estimates that skimming costs consumers and financial institutions more than $1 billion each year. The agency has also stepped up its nationwide enforcement efforts. During 2025 operations, law enforcement removed more than 400 illegal skimming devices. The Secret Service says skimming activity has increasingly targeted EBT cards. A recent Los Angeles sweep shows how widespread the problem has become. Law enforcement visited 328 businesses and inspected 1,749 payment devices. Agents seized 16 skimmers. The Secret Service estimated those removals prevented about $16.6 million in potential fraud losses. Why criminals are targeting EBT cards This is where things take a troubling turn. The Secret Service says criminals intentionally target locations with heavy EBT use. That includes stores where people use government benefits to buy groceries. Many credit and debit cards now offer chips or contactless payment. However, many EBT transactions still require a magnetic-stripe swipe. That gives criminals an opening. A skimmer can capture the information stored on the magnetic stripe. Criminals can then copy that information onto another magnetic-stripe card. If they also capture the victim's PIN, they can use the cloned card to steal benefits. For people who rely on those benefits, the impact can be immediate. Victims may discover their accounts have been drained when they try to buy groceries or pay for everyday necessities. Recovering stolen benefits can also take time, leaving families without money they were counting on. VENEZUELAN NATIONALS CHARGED IN $529K ATM JACKPOTTING SCHEME AT I-95 REST STOPS, FEDS SAY Why EBT card security is changing Federal officials know the magnetic stripe is a weak point. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food and Nutrition Service says EBT fraud involving skimming is rising. The agency is working with states on modernizing SNAP EBT systems, including introducing chip cards. Chip technology makes card information harder to copy than data stored on a magnetic stripe. Still, that transition takes time. Until more EBT systems support newer payment technology, millions of people may continue using cards that require a swipe. That leaves benefit recipients with fewer ways to avoid the very payment method criminals are targeting. Organized crime groups are behind some skimming operations The Secret Service says organized criminal groups are involved in some of these skimming schemes. Investigators have linked some operations to groups that travel into the United States and move between locations installing devices. The agency has been conducting skimming operations across the country throughout 2026. Recent sweeps have focused on payment terminals at stores and ATMs where skimming activity is suspected. That kind of coordinated activity can make the devices harder to track and allow criminals to target multiple locations in a short period of time. How to protect yourself from card skimmers You may never spot a well-made skimmer by sight alone. Still, you can lower your risk and catch suspicious activity faster. 1) Tap instead of swiping when you can If a payment terminal supports contactless payments, use them. The Secret Service recommends tap-to-pay when possible. You can also use a digital wallet on your phone if the retailer supports it. For more ways to protect your cards in stores and online, see our guide on how to protect your credit and bank cards from getting hacked. 2) Inspect the payment terminal first Take a few seconds before inserting or swiping your card. Look for a reader that appears loose or crooked. Also watch for damage, unusual gaps or parts that do not seem to line up correctly. The Secret Service recommends avoiding a reader if something looks altered or damaged. IDENTITY THEFT RARELY ANNOUNCES ITSELF: 6 SIGNS YOU MISSED 3) Give the reader a gentle pull Some overlay skimmers sit directly on top of the legitimate card reader. Before swiping, gently check whether anything feels loose or moves unexpectedly. Do not try to rip apart a terminal. If something seems suspicious, stop using it and notify the store. 4) Cover the keypad when entering your PIN A skimmer may capture card information while another device records your PIN. Use your hand to shield the keypad whenever you enter a PIN. That simple habit can make captured card information less useful to a criminal. 5) Turn on transaction alerts Enable alerts through your bank or card issuer so you know when your card gets used. Pay attention to small charges too. If you see something you do not recognize, contact your financial institution using the number on your card or its official app. If money has already disappeared from an account, follow our steps on what to do if your bank account is hacked. 6) Check your EBT balance regularly EBT users should review their account history for transactions they do not recognize. The Food and Nutrition Service recommends checking EBT accounts regularly. It also advises changing your PIN at least once a month, particularly before your benefits are issued. If you spot an unauthorized transaction, change your PIN immediately and contact your state EBT agency. 7) Never share your EBT PIN Government agencies should not need your PIN to verify your eligibility. Do not provide your EBT card number or PIN in response to an unexpected text, phone call or email. Federal officials warn that criminals use several methods to steal benefit information, so protecting the PIN remains important even when no physical skimmer is involved. What to do if you think a skimmer stole your card information Act quickly once you notice suspicious transactions. Kurt's key takeaways What bothers me most about this scam is that criminals are going after people who may have the fewest options to protect themselves. If I can tap my credit card or pay with my phone, I can avoid swiping altogether. Many EBT users cannot make that same choice because their cards still rely on older magnetic-stripe technology. That needs to change. These skimmers have become convincing enough to fool almost anyone, and some can transmit stolen information without the criminal ever coming back for the device. You can check the reader and keep an eye on your account, but there is only so much you can do when the payment system itself leaves you exposed. Moving benefit cards to more secure technology should be a priority, especially when families are depending on that money for food. articles.title: How Trump’s DOJ reached a shocking settlement with Live Nation-Ticketmaster.
articles.summary:
The Wall Street Journal has a rundown on the behind-the-scenes wrangling that led to the baffling settlement agreement earlier this year, and left state AGs to pursue their own case. In an unusual twist, the settlement talks happened at the White House, with the AG and the White House lawyer, before giving the states a day to decide whether to join the deal. None did.
And at the end:
> The following month, Trump nominated McDonald—the Sullivan & Cromwell lawyer who had represented Live Nation in the settlement—to be Manhattan’s top federal prosecutor.

articles.title: Adiós al Código 78: la DGT ultima un cambio clave para el carnet de conducir que empieza en la autoescuela
articles.standfirst: Hasta hoy, si te sacas el carnet con un coche automático no puedes conducir manuales... pero eso va a cambiar
articles.summary: Hasta hoy, si te sacas el carnet con un coche automático no puedes conducir manuales... pero eso va a cambiar
articles.body: Actualmente hay dos modalidades para el obtener el permiso de conducción B para turismos: la convencional, mediante un vehículo con transmisión manual o una alternativa, si realizas las prácticas y el examen con un modelo con cambio automático, sin pedal de embrague. En el segundo de los casos, a los poseedores del permiso B se les incluye el llamado Código 78 que indica a las autoridades que no pueden manejar vehículos, digamos, 'convencionales'. Sin embargo, la realidad del mundo del automóvil está haciendo que, precisamente, lo 'convencional' ahora sean los coches con caja de cambios automáitca, sobre todo según va avanzando la electrificación. Los coches híbridos, híbridos enchufables y eléctricos tienen este tipo de transmisión en la que un mecanismo, en función de la situación de conducción y de los datos de los sensores del motor y de los sistemas electrónicos, ejecuta los cambios de marcha en función de la eficiencia y, en ocasiones, de la tracción. Hoy por hoy, las autoescuelas siguen recibiendo una inmensa mayoría de peticiones para obtener el carnet B con coches con cambio manual (un 95 por ciento) -tal como reconoce la DGT en su último número de la Revista Tráfico-, pero eso va a cambiar a corto plazo. Porque Tráfico ya trabaja con un cambio de normativa en el que el Cógido 78 desaparezca y, en su lugar, haya un camino diferente para que los que obtengan el carnet con un coche automático puedan conducir también los manuales. Y eso puede cambiarlo todo. La DGT establecerá como requisito un curso adicional, que en principio consistirá en un mínimo de siete horas de prácticas con coches manuales, para que exista la convalidación de ese Código 78.  La adopción de esta medida, además de para adecuar al conductor a la realidad de la industria automotriz (en la que los cambios manuales), se aplica para fomentar los vehículos electrificados. Incluso desde la Confederación Nacional de Autoescuelas (CNAE) se aplaude la iniciativa ya que se considera que con el cambio "el automático se convertirá en la principal puerta de entrada principal a la conducción". Desde tráfico y las autoescuelas se considera, además, que los coches automáticos tienen grandes ventajas ya que centra la atención del conductor en la carretera. Igualmente, los coches automáticos son más precisos y rápidos en los cambios de marchas y conllevan ventajas ecológicas (consumen y contaminan menos al gestionar la transmisión de forma más eficiente).

articles.title: AI-powered hackers: The new cyberwar is faster, smarter & harder to stop
articles.summary: News News: Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming a tool for cyberattacks, helping hackers automate tasks, move faster and coordinate complex operation.
articles.body: Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming a tool for cyberattacks, helping hackers automate tasks, move faster and coordinate complex operations.The result is a growing concern among cybersecurity experts: Has AI made it significantly easier to breach web systems?One of the most prominent recent examples emerged in July, when Taiwan's government agencies faced what officials described as a massive and unprecedented cyberattack. Taiwan's ministry of digital affairs said its monitoring systems detected the intrusion, triggering warnings and an investigation.Officials concluded that the attackers had combined conventional manual hacking with AI agents, including one reportedly called OpenClaw.According to Israeli cybersecurity firm Dream, the operation compromised nearly 21 government systems, breached 85 user accounts and extracted about 2,500 personnel records. The targets reportedly included Taiwan's justice ministry, nuclear safety agency and several energy companies."Thereâs still a human in there somewhere," Cris Thomas, a security researcher at Semgrep, told Reuters. "Somebody had to choose who to attack, had to establish an objective and give it a directive. Itâs not totally 100% autonomous. There was a capable operator in charge that did that."Taiwan, however, was not an isolated case.On November 13, 2025, Anthropic disclosed what it described as the first documented large-scale cyberattack carried out mostly without direct human involvement. The company said a state-linked group manipulated its Claude Code tool into attacking roughly 30 organisations worldwide, including financial institutions.The attackers reportedly broke the operation into small tasks and presented themselves as a legitimate cybersecurity firm conducting defensive tests. Anthropic estimated that AI performed 80% to 90% of the campaign, with humans intervening at only four to six critical decision points. At its peak, the system generated multiple requests every second, operating at a scale no human team could match.The significance of both cases lies not in AI independently "hacking the internet", but in its ability to connect and automate different stages of an attack: reconnaissance, credential theft, vulnerability discovery and movement through a network. All while a human sets the broader objective.How AI is lowering the barrier to cyberattacksAI has not reinvented cybercrime. What it has done is reduce the expertise, time and repetitive effort required to carry out many existing attack techniques.Prof Amgoth Tarachand of the Indian Institute of Technology (ISM) Dhanbad told TOI that AI can reduce the knowledge and labour traditionally required at different stages of an attack, without eliminating the need for human judgement or an actual path into the target.At its simplest, AI acts as an assistant: explaining unfamiliar code, drafting phishing messages or answering technical questions that would otherwise require hours of research.As an automation layer, it can handle repetitive work such as scanning, generating scripts and sorting data at speeds far beyond a human operator. As an agent, it can chain several tasks together towards an objective set by a human, checking back only when necessary.But that does not make cyberattacks fully autonomous."Cyberattacks are not simply programming problems," Amgoth said. "Successful operations require judgment: choosing targets, understanding unusual system behaviour, distinguishing genuine vulnerabilities from false positives, maintaining access, avoiding detection, and knowing what to do when circumstances change."AI can still make mistakes, misunderstand systems and confidently produce incorrect answers.A separate line of evidence points to the same shift. A report published this year by India's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) describes attackers moving from manual, specialist operations towards repeatable, automated attack pipelines. Reconnaissance, exploit chaining and payload delivery are increasingly being industrialised "more like software manufacturing than tradecraft".The report also notes that AI removes human bandwidth as a constraint, allowing attackers to run multiple operations simultaneously without the fatigue and time limitations faced by human teams.Anthropic's own research illustrates the trend. The company reviewed 832 accounts linked to malicious activity between March 2025 and March 2026 and found AI being used across all 14 broad attack tactics in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, the industry's standard map of adversarial techniques. Anthropic said the proportion of those accounts rated medium-risk or higher increased from 33% to 56% during the period.On April 7, 2026, Anthropic also said its Claude Mythos Preview model had identified more than 23,000 potential software vulnerabilities during internal testing, including more than 1,000 rated high or critical severity. The company described the result as a "structural shift" from the capabilities of earlier models.These are Anthropic's own findings rather than independent measurements of what routinely happens across the internet. But they indicate that the technical ceiling of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery is rising rapidly.For Amgoth, the bigger change may be who can conduct a sophisticated operation."The long-term threat may not be 'AI teaches more people to hack,'" he said. "It may instead be one moderately skilled operator supervising what previously required a team of specialists."The shift is already visible in social engineering. Microsoft has reported an increase in the scale and sophistication of AI-assisted phishing, while Google has documented attackers using generative AI to create convincing, multilingual phishing messages, eliminating grammatical mistakes that once helped users identify scams."AI is converting expertise into a service and time into computation," Amgoth said. "Knowledge that previously took years to accumulate can increasingly be accessed on demand, and work that took hours can sometimes be compressed into minutes."That is what lowering the barrier really means. AI does not magically turn an inexperienced person into an elite hacker. It can, however, remove much of the slow, repetitive work that separates a moderately skilled operator from a much more capable team.Also read | Asked to solve a lab test, AI hacked the internet instead: When agents start doing things nobody told them to doCan anyone with AI hack into a web system?No.Having a web address and access to an AI chatbot does not mean someone can simply break into the system behind it. A URL tells an attacker where the door is. It does not give them the key.Given only a link, AI can help analyse a website from the outside, identifying technologies, explaining technical terminology and highlighting known weaknesses in software components it can detect. Google reported in May 2026 that threat actors were increasingly using AI to accelerate this kind of early-stage research."The URL tells the attacker where the door is. AI may help them examine the door far more intelligently, but there still has to be a weakness in the lock, a stolen key, or somebody willing to open it," Amgoth said.Google has also described a separate case involving a threat actor that used a zero-day exploit, a previously unknown software vulnerability, that the company believed had been developed with AI assistance.The frontier is clearly moving. But that does not mean every website is suddenly vulnerable because powerful AI exists. Real-world systems still rely on authentication, access controls, monitoring, rate limits, network segmentation and security patches. AI, meanwhile, remains capable of making basic mistakes.The critical change is therefore not that AI has removed the technical barriers to hacking. It has lowered some of the barriers surrounding them.AI for cyberdefenceThe same capabilities that make AI useful to attackers can give defenders a powerful advantage.Amgoth describes AI in cybersecurity as a force multiplier rather than a replacement for human defenders. The crucial advantage for defenders is access to information that an outside attacker normally does not have."While an attacker normally has only fragments of information about a web system, the defender can give AI visibility across the source code, software dependencies, identities, network activity, cloud infrastructure, application logs and organisational threat intelligence simultaneously," he said.That broader visibility can make AI particularly useful for finding vulnerabilities, detecting unusual behaviour and identifying attack patterns.In February 2026, Anthropic reported that its models could identify previously unknown, high-severity vulnerabilities in mature, well-tested codebases and described a system that could scan repositories and suggest patches for human review.Google's Mandiant division reported in August 2026 that it had developed a similar agentic approach to source-code review, using it in penetration testing and incident response.AI-assisted monitoring can also process enormous volumes of security data much faster than human analysts working through logs manually. CERT-In's report, particularly in the context of the financial sector, describes a shift from periodic security checks towards continuous monitoring because attackers operating at machine speed cannot be reliably countered by reviews conducted once a quarter.But AI-driven defence comes with its own risks. Giving an AI system broad access to source code, cloud infrastructure or credentials creates a new potential point of failure if the system is poorly controlled. Google's Mandiant team has also warned about the risks associated with deploying privileged AI agents without appropriate safeguards.The balance, therefore, is not simply between hackers and AI.It is between AI-assisted attackers and AI-assisted defenders.The Taiwan attack and Anthropic's disclosure demonstrate how AI can allow attackers to accomplish more with fewer people and less time. Faster code analysis, faster reconnaissance and faster iteration can turn what once required a team of specialists into a much more automated operation.But those same capabilities are available to defenders, and defenders typically have access to far more information about their own systems than an attacker can obtain from the outside.The barrier is falling on both sides.The question is no longer whether AI will make cyberattacks easier. It already has for many stages of an operation. The bigger question is who will use AI more effectively, the attacker trying to exploit a weakness or the defender trying to plug it?

Faster code analysis, faster reconnaissance and faster iteration can turn what once required a team of specialists into a much more automated operation.But those same capabilities are available to defenders, and defenders typically have access to far more information about their own systems than an attacker can obtain from the outside.The barrier is falling on both sides.The question is no longer whether AI will make cyberattacks easier. It already has for many stages of an operation. The bigger question is who will use AI more effectively, the attacker trying to exploit a weakness or the defender trying to plug it?

articles.title: Trump plans to grow his way out of $40 trillion debt crisis—it’s a ‘fantastic story’ but virtually impossible, says top budget economist
articles.summary: "If you tell the debt markets: 'Hey, we think we're gonna be able to grow our way out of this,' and then a year later they're not seeing any improvements fro...
articles.body:
The U.S. national debt has hit $40 trillion , and the Trump administration is facing questions about its budget plans as a result. The good news is, there has one: The American economy will apparently grow its way out of any fiscal crisis. "It's been a problem for 35 years," Trump told reporters Friday. "And what we have now … is we have tremendous growth. And the way you take care of debt is with growth, and we have tremendous growth. We've never had growth like we have right now." "There's nothing magic about the $40 trillion number," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CNBC last week, "And we can grow our way out of that."

Economists would be inclined to agree with Bessent: The value of the debt, while an extraordinary milestone, doesn't hold much relative weight. What economists (and more importantly, the bond market) is watching is the debt-to-GDP ratio: This demonstrates the level of borrowing by a country against its economic capacity to repay and service it.

Currently, the U.S. ratio stands at 122%. To bring it back into a lower balance, an economy could cut its borrowing or—as Bessent suggests—increase its growth.

When the alternative is cutting borrowing and, as a result, government spending, the growth plan is a more optimistic and politically palatable route.

It's also the latest in a series of solutions proposed by the White House: Originally, President Trump had suggested that tariffs would pay down the national debt (the plan was quickly nixed by a Supreme Court ruling ordering the administration to repay approximately $100 billion in revenues that the justices deemed illegal).

Trump later suggested a "golden visa" strategy —selling rich immigrants visas at $5 million each—could pay down the national debt. The policies were novel, but economists broadly welcomed action by the Trump Administration on the fiscal picture.

But now there a bond market reckoning looming. The risk premium demanded by investors for holding the 30-year Treasury rose to over 5.3% in recent days, prompting U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to deploy $4 billion or more in unscheduled buybacks. If the U.S. can't pay its debt, the worst-case scenario is a default crisis.

So, can the U.S. grow its way out of debt? It's a "fantastic story," says Kent Smetters , Boettner Professor of economics and public policy at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania.

Unfortunately, Professor Smetters—the faculty director of a fiscal analysis tool called the Penn Wharton Budget Model—says the plan is also "pretty clearly" not feasible. He explained in an interview with Fortune : "People often get the causality kind of opposite. They think more growth, less of a debt problem, and in reality, it's just the opposite … We deal with the debt issue in order to try to aid economic growth, not vice versa."

articles.title: WhatsApp tightens account security with stronger two-step verification and more | TechCrunch
articles.summary: WhatsApp’s two-step verification previously relied on a six-digit PIN, but now users can choose a longer, alphanumeric password with special characters.
articles.body:
WhatsApp announced Tuesday that it’s launching new security features and updates to help users keep their accounts secure, including stronger two-step verification and the ability to add more than one passkey to your account. The Meta-owned app is also adding context to calls from unknown numbers.

The updates come as WhatsApp and other messaging apps, such as Signal and Telegram , look to make account security easier and more accessible for everyday users, especially as phishing and hacking attempts have become more sophisticated over the years.

Until now, WhatsApp’s two-step verification has used a six-digit PIN as an extra layer of protection to prevent someone from taking over an account even if they’re able to obtain the user’s one-time passcode. Now, users can choose a longer, alphanumeric password with special characters to make the PIN harder to guess.

As for passkeys, users can now add more than one passkey to their account, which WhatsApps says will be useful if a person uses both iOS and Android.

Passkeys, which WhatsApp launched support for in 2024 , are far stronger than passwords and allow users to log in to their accounts using Face ID or their fingerprint. Passkeys remove the need to rely on username and password combinations, which are ordinarily susceptible to phishing attacks. Passkey logins make it harder for bad actors to remotely access your accounts, as an attacker would need physical access to a person’s device that stores the user’s part of the passkey.

Additionally, Android users will now see more information when they’re getting a call from someone who isn’t in their contacts, like whether the number is from a different country and if they have any groups in common with the caller.

The latest features join the growing list of updates WhatsApp has rolled out in recent months. The company launched usernames in late June to allow people to share their profiles without disclosing their phone number. In late May, Meta launched a subscription plan for the messaging app that unlocks extra features, like profile customization, super reactions, story insights, and more.

The WhatsApp Plus plan launched alongside similar “Plus” offerings for Instagram and Facebook.

articles.title: It cost billionaire Joe Lonsdale less than $15M a year to rewrite America's homelessness playbook, calls it 'very small'
articles.summary: For less than $15 million a year, Joe Lonsdale's think tank has helped rewrite homelessness policy in 16 states and reshape the Trump administration's approa...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump is looking to overhaul the federal homelessness policy, moving away from housing subsidies and toward mandatory treatment for people struggling with mental illness or substance abuse. The administration is also pursuing policies that would make sleeping or camping on public streets illegal.

According to the New York Times , the shift has been heavily influenced by one organization — and one billionaire.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

A team from Cicero Institute , a think tank founded by billionaire and Trump ally Joe Lonsdale, has traveled across the country pushing lawmakers to criminalize public camping and sleeping on streets.

According to the New York Times, 21 states have considered camping bans or other homelessness laws backed by Cicero, with 16 ultimately passing them. The group is now working with the Trump administration to redirect federal funding away from housing subsidies and toward forced treatment programs.

Homelessness has neared record highs. In January 2025 , when Trump took office for his second term, nearly 746,000 people were experiencing homelessness. The increase has led some Republicans to embrace tougher measures to clear streets and, according to the New York Times, no group has pushed harder than Cicero Institute.

The group's central target is Housing First , the current federal policy on homelessness. The measure prioritizes getting people into stable housing before addressing issues such as addiction or mental health. The policy was embraced by Trump during his first term. The administration now argues the policy ignores the root cause of homelessness by providing housing subsidies but making treatment optional — a sentiment backed by Cicero.

Critics, however, argue that housing is itself a crucial first step in helping people stabilize their lives and that there is limited evidence that forcing people into treatment will reduce homelessness.

In July 2025, the administration issued an executive order called "Ending Crime and Disorder on American Streets," which includes a camping ban.

"Obviously, our work has been one of the main influences" in shaping administration views, Mr. Lonsdale said in an interview with the New York Times .

articles.title: Biden Added $8 Trillion To The National Debt Making Him The 3rd Biggest Spending President. You Can Probably Guess Who Is #1
articles.summary: With federal debt crossing $40 trillion, analysts are ranking presidents by how much they borrowed, and the results challenge some popular assumptions about...
articles.body:
Trump leads recent presidents with $12 trillion in combined debt added, followed by Obama at $9 trillion and Biden at $8 trillion.

Biden's single term added more debt than Trump's entire first term, placing him third only because Trump's two terms are combined.

Mandatory spending and interest payments now consume over 60% of the federal budget, with interest costs alone exceeding Pentagon funding.

Don't wait: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just revealed his top 10 AI stocks. See the full list FREE now .

Federal debt outstanding crossed $40 trillion on or around Aug. 19, 2026. That doubling has revived ranking presidents by debt added. Using Treasury's "Debt to the Penny" series from start to end of term in nominal dollars, Joe Biden's single term added roughly $8.45 trillion, placing him third among the last five presidents. Donald Trump ranks first; Barack Obama second.

Measured by actual increase in total public debt outstanding: Trump, both terms combined, roughly $11.63 trillion, of which roughly $7.80 trillion came in term one and roughly $3.83 trillion in the first 19 months of term two; Obama, two terms, roughly $9.32 trillion; Biden, one term, roughly $8.45 trillion; George W. Bush, two terms, roughly $4.90 trillion; and Reagan, two terms, roughly $1.86 trillion.

Trump ranks first because his two non-consecutive terms are combined. Measured term by term, Biden's roughly $8.45 trillion exceeds Trump's first term of roughly $7.80 trillion. His second term is still in progress, so his total will keep growing and is not a finished, comparable number like the others. Combining terms is a legitimate approach and the one Newsweek used in its Aug. 20, 2026 analysis, which independently produced essentially the same totals.

The "$8 trillion" is rounded shorthand for the roughly $8.45 trillion Treasury figure. A debt increase reflects the gap between spending and revenue plus other financing needs, not spending alone. Tax cuts, revenue shortfalls, and interest costs each contribute independently. "Spending president" is common shorthand; the label is imprecise.

A separate measurement matters. The nonpartisan Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, in an April 3, 2025 analysis, estimated that Biden-era legislation and executive actions added a projected $4.7 trillion in new debt over a 10-year window, scored at enactment. That figure differs from Treasury's $8.45 trillion. CRFB counts only new policy choices as scored at enactment; it excludes pre-existing mandatory spending growth, revenue performance, and rising interest costs on existing debt. The two figures are not in conflict.

articles.title: Apple rescues Hide My Email feature from the privacy scrap heap
articles.summary: Apple says it will no longer ditch using its icloud.com domain for hiding people's email addresses.
articles.body:
Apple has reneged on a planned change to its Hide My Email feature that users said would have made the privacy tool less effective.

Hide My Email is a privacy feature for paying iCloud+ users that generates a unique and disposable email address to give websites instead of a person’s real email address and still have emails route to their regular inboxes. The benefit of the email-hiding feature is that privately generated email addresses cannot be distinguished from regular Apple users with an @icloud.com email address. However, the feature still allows Apple to tell law enforcement who is behind a masked email address .

Earlier this year, the company said it would move users to @private.icloud.com , which users said would make it easier for websites to reject these email addresses during sign-ups. On social media and Reddit threads, users criticized the change as defeating the purpose of the service altogether.

The company confirmed an update on Monday that Hide My Email addresses “will remain” on @icloud.com , after previously saying it would move users to @private.icloud.com .

Apple did not give a reason for changing its decision, but Daring Fireball’s John Gruber , who first reported the about-face, said that Apple employees had objected to the change all along.

Earlier this year, 404 Media reported that a bug in Hide My Email revealed people’s real email addresses. Apple fixed the bug more than a year after it was first made aware that emails rejected as spam would leak the masked users’ real email addresses.

articles.title: JPMorgan compares Bessent's $4B bond buyback to 'paying your mortgage with your credit card' as U.S. debt hits $40T
articles.summary: The bond market is a mess, but what do all the recent developments mean?
articles.body:
Debt by any other name is still debt, and if you've ever been in any amount of it, you'll know that the one thing that is definitely not the solution is, well, even more debt. And yet, that seems to be the preferred strategy of modern governments: If more money is needed, then they can simply fund it with endless debt.

The level of arrears accrued by the powers of the world is almost incomprehensible at this point. According to the Institute of International Finance, total global debt , across sectors and types of lending, is over $350 trillion, equivalent to about 305% of global GDP. That's compared to 240% of GDP in 2005.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

Our comfort with using borrowed money is why, perhaps, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is so confident in his latest scheme to curb concerns over waning demand for bonds — buying back more of the debt to simply reissue it under different terms.

The plan, outlined late last week , is intended to improve market conditions by soaking up longer-term bonds with high yield rates as people become increasingly wary of how the investment vehicles will perform in these economically uncertain times.

The problem with the buyback is the fact that the Treasury will issue shorter-term bonds to pay for it, which, according to JPMorgan's James Sullivan, is akin to "paying your mortgage with your credit card" as it "can work for a while, but eventually the mismatch starts to become more obvious."

Sullivan, who serves as the firm's co-head of global fundamental research, made the comparison on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Aug. 21 , warning that the Treasury is only deferring the problem of the glaring debt to a later date. Though the department is unfortunately quite limited in how it can deal with the situation in any meaningful capacity, experts remain critical of the temporary fix.

Instant effects — but what about long-term?

The announcement had the effect of immediately pushing 30-year treasury yields — which had reached a ceiling of 5.34% last week, the highest seen in 19 years — to 5.18% , though they have since risen back to close to 5.25% .

Some argue that the unexpected timing of the action was the action, including Padhraic Garvey, ING bank's Head of American Research, who admits that though the recovery will merely "dampen but not abort the pressure."

articles.title: That fake Grand Theft Auto VI demo is actually just malware | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Grand Theft Auto fans, eager for news about one of the most anticipated video games of all time, appear especially vulnerable to this new cyberattack.
articles.body:
In the long wait for the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI, an open-world game about crime, some in the gaming community are being targeted by cybercriminals in the real world.

Fans are still waiting for the game more than a decade after the release of GTA 5, which sold more copies than any game ever, except for Minecraft. Now, after multiple GTA 6 delays and with some fans desperate for any scrap of news, hackers are using the cover as a perfect opportunity to target eager gamers.

Cybercriminals have created fake websites impersonating Rockstar, the developer behind GTA 6. These websites advertise a playable GTA 6 demo — but no legitimate demo exists. Once the unsuspecting gamer clicks the “Play Now” button, they download a file that looks like a game installer, but is actually malware, according to the cybersecurity company Malwarebytes .

The malware is an information stealer that is designed to find and take a victim’s passwords, cookies, and logged-in sessions stored in their web browser. These attacks can in some cases allow hackers to log in as if they were the account holder, even when protected by multi-factor authentication.

After multiple delays, GTA 6 is expected to release on November 19, 2026. On Thursday, Netflix will air an extended look at the game, which could perhaps answer some questions about the legitimacy of various leaks.

A relevant reminder as always: Don’t download stuff if you aren’t sure it comes from a reliable source.

articles.title: Google Docs password leak reveals a costly security mistake
articles.summary: A contractor stored credentials in a Google Doc set to "Anyone with the link," and Google Search autocomplete eventually surfaced the password string.
articles.body: Passwords have a way of ending up in places they were never meant to live. Sometimes convenience wins in the moment, and security becomes tomorrow's problem. One company learned that lesson after a contractor stored credentials in a Google Doc so they could access them from different devices. Then something happened that should make anyone who uses Google Docs take a closer look at their sharing settings. A developer searching the company's domain on Google saw one of its staging hostnames appear in autocomplete alongside what looked like a credential string. The company investigated and found a Google Docs URL that anyone with the link could access. That's a rough way to discover that a password has traveled much farther than you intended. Here's how the exposure happened, what Google says about Docs privacy and the simple steps you can take to keep your own passwords and shared files safer. New! articles.title: Trump is upping the price of Big Tech’s favorite visa
articles.summary: The Trump administration has transformed the once-mundane visa system into a tool for going after immigrants.
articles.body: In the span of a few hours on Monday, the Department of Homeland Security announced that it would be implementing a fee of over $103,000 on H-1B visas, and news broke that the State Department plans on revoking the visas of up to 200,000 asylum seekers — which, according to The Associated Press, would be the largest mass visa revocation in US history.  More than a year into President Donald Trump’s second term, it’s become clear that the only way Trump can get the deportation numbers he wants is by stripping legal immigrants of status. Beyond having ICE arrest, detain, and deport immigrants, the administration is pressuring noncitizens to “self-deport,” in some cases imposing civil fines on them and threatening to seize their assets. It’s creating legal hurdles not only for new legal immigrants but for those already in the country, and in the process, likely hurting businesses and social services nationwide. H-1B visas are often seen as synonymous with Big Tech, in no small part because Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft are the three biggest employers of H-1B workers. A federal judge struck down Trump’s previous attempt to raise the cost of these high-skilled employment visas in June, but not until over 70 employers paid the $100,000 fee. Now Trump wants to raise the cost to $103,265. Advocates and business leaders are worried Trump will soon come after the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, which DHS hinted may soon carry a $100,000 fee of its own. OPT lets international students work in their field of study for 12 months, with extensions of up to 24 months for some STEM students and additional extensions for holders of certain graduate degrees. “This is clearly unlawful,” said Todd Schulte, the president of FWD.us, an immigration reform organization founded by Mark Zuckerberg and other tech executives in 2013. “We don’t have to guess what this is for. This is to get rid of the OPT and H-1B program, which will have upstream and downstream devastating consequences: companies will be started elsewhere, people will be hired elsewhere.” This won’t just hurt the tech industry. The previous fee hike exacerbated labor shortages at rural hospitals across the country and Alaska public schools, both of which have increasingly turned to high-skilled immigrant workers in the wake of local population decline. If the $100,000 fee was an inconvenience for Amazon and Meta, it was utterly catastrophic for rural communities already having trouble attracting qualified candidates.  Foreign workers aren’t the only legal immigrants Trump is targeting. According to the AP, which broke the news, the State Department will rescind up to 200,000 business and travel visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to people who applied for asylum after arriving in the US. Beyond limiting their ability to travel outside the country, this move won’t change much for asylum seekers who came to the US on nonimmigrant visas — at least not for now. But Schulte said the visa revocations are part of Trump’s efforts to gut the humanitarian immigration system. “Every single other pathway is harder, outlawed, eliminated, more bureaucratic, more difficult across the board,” he said. “It’s an all-of-government approach.” The administration is framing this change as a way of closing a loophole in the asylum system: people coming to the country on nonimmigrant visas, ostensibly for work or pleasure, only to ask for asylum upon setting foot in the country. “We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told the AP. But the people who applied for asylum this way didn’t break any laws. In fact, a person needs to be present on US soil to apply for asylum; there’s no way to apply from outside the country. And Trump has closed most other avenues for humanitarian migration. There’s an effective “asylum ban” in place at the US-Mexico border. Refugee admissions have dropped to record lows, and the administration is now prioritizing the resettlement of white South Africans and denying almost everyone else.  In his second term, Trump has shown that the only immigrants he wants are those who look a certain way — or who can pay a small fortune for the privilege of working in America.

articles.title: Japan's corporate services inflation accelerates in July
articles.summary: TOKYO, Aug 26 (Reuters) - A key gauge of Japan's service-sector inflation rose 3.6% in July from a year earlier, data showed on Wednesday, reinforcing the ce...
articles.body:
TOKYO, Aug 26 (Reuters) - A key gauge of Japan's service-sector inflation rose ‌3.6% in July from a year ‌earlier, data showed on Wednesday, reinforcing the central ​bank's view that a tight labour market is pushing firms to pass rising costs on to consumers.

The increase in the services ‌producer price ⁠index, which tracks the prices companies charge each other for services, ⁠followed a revised 3.4% gain in June, Bank of Japan data showed.

The data ​added to ​signs of broadening ​inflationary pressure in the ‌economy that have bolstered the case for a near-term interest rate hike.

Japan's core consumer inflation accelerated in July from a year earlier as firms passed on ‌rising import costs from a ​weak yen and the ​U.S.-Israeli war ​with Iran.

Sources have told Reuters ‌the BOJ is set ​to raise ​the rate as soon as September and is considering hiking more aggressively thereafter ​from ‌the current pace of roughly two times ​a year.

(Reporting by Leika Kihara; ​Editing by Jacqueline Wong)
